title: Research Bite #61: A Scoping Review of 20 Years of Research on Differentiation
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #61 covers Linda Graham, Kate de Bruin, Carly Lassig, and Ilektra Spandagou's 'A scoping review of 20 years of research on differentiation: investigating conceptualisation, characteristics, and methods used,' published in Review of Education (2021, Vol. 9, No. 1, Article 3238). Using PRISMA-guided systematic screening, the team narrowed a broad literature search down to 34 peer-reviewed studies on classroom differentiation published between 1999 and 2019, about half conducted in the United States and most concentrated in elementary school. The headline finding is not about whether differentiation works, but about how incoherently the field has defined it: the term 'differentiation' is used to describe genuinely incompatible practices, including ability streaming and outright segregation, alongside more defensible responsive-teaching approaches. Most of the reviewed studies examined teacher perceptions and practices rather than measuring actual student outcomes, and survey and case-study designs dominated the methodology. The authors conclude that the evidence base is fragmented precisely because there is no shared operational definition of differentiation to build a coherent research program around.
points: The review's central finding -- that 'differentiation' is used to label practices as different as ability streaming and responsive individualized teaching -- means any claim that 'differentiation is evidence-based' should be treated with suspicion until the specific practice is named.

Only a minority of the 34 studies actually measured student outcomes; most examined teacher perceptions and practices, meaning the field knows more about how teachers talk about differentiation than about whether it works.

The geographic and phase concentration (roughly half U.S.-based, mostly elementary) means the existing evidence base may not generalize well to secondary or non-U.S. contexts, a gap the authors flag directly.

Because the review spans two full decades (1999-2019) and still finds no standardized definition, this is not a temporary growing-pain problem -- it is a structural weakness in how the field studies differentiation.

The authors' call for standardised definitions is itself the most actionable takeaway: schools evaluating a 'differentiation' initiative should first pin down exactly which practice is meant before assuming research support transfers.
quotes: This scoping review examines twenty years of academic research on the educational practice of differentiation, a method used to address student diversity in mainstream classrooms.
The authors analysed 34 peer-reviewed studies published between 1999 and 2019 to understand how this pedagogical approach is defined, implemented, and measured.
Their findings reveal significant terminological confusion, noting that the term is frequently applied to incompatible practices like ability streaming or segregation.
While many studies focus on teacher perceptions and practices in elementary settings, very few rigorously investigate the specific impact on student outcomes.

Ultimately, the review highlights a fragmented evidence base caused by diverse methodologies and inconsistent conceptual frameworks. Consequently, the authors suggest that standardised definitions and more robust research are necessary.
